reader_summary.headline: Welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
reader_summary.overview: Welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye. I'm your host, Niklas Savos, and next to me is my friend, Eddie Palngren. It's really a fairy tale day here in Stockholm. Mine is 15 degrees, snow everywhere, and the sun is about to set, although it's just 2 p.m.

key_points.text: But I'm really excited, because today we will talk with Chris Mayer, co-founder and portfolio manager at Woodlock House Family Capital.
key_points.evidence_quote: But I'm really excited, because today we will talk with Chris Mayer, co-founder and portfolio manager at Woodlock House Family Capital, and the author of multiple books.

key_points.text: The one he's most famous for is probably the one we will discuss today, 100 Baggers.
key_points.evidence_quote: The one he's most famous for is probably the one we will discuss today, 100 Baggers, which is a study of the best-performing US stocks, that each, for every $10,000 invested, have returned $1 million and often more.

key_points.text: And the publisher spent $50,000 just to get the data, which spans from 1962 to 2014.
key_points.evidence_quote: And the publisher spent $50,000 just to get the data, which spans from 1962 to 2014, and it resulted in 365 stocks that returned 100-fold or more.

key_points.text: And the largest inspiration for Chris to write a book was Thomas Phelps.
key_points.evidence_quote: And the largest inspiration for Chris to write a book was Thomas Phelps.

positions.commentary: The speaker describes Copart as a founder-led company where the CEO came up from the business, starting as a teenager and now running the show.
The speaker cites Old Dominion Freight Line as an example of an 'invisible moat' built around culture, highlighting its long-term high returns on capital and ability to outperform peers.
The speaker mentions Brown and Brown as a company that checks all the boxes from a people standpoint, noting the CEO is third-generation and the CFO is thoughtful.

thesis: This episode argues that high returns on capital are often driven by durable competitive advantages, which can be physical (like Copart's yards) or cultural (like Old Dominion's people-centric model). It further suggests that founder-led companies with strong management teams, such as Brown & Brown, represent high-quality investment opportunities.

claims.claim: The speaker considers Copart a good example of a company with a physical moat, noting its difficult-to-replicate yards and long-term high returns on capital.
claims.quote: I mentioned Copart before. They have a moat that is more of a physical moat. So it's a good example to use because it's easier to understand. You know, they have these huge yards where they have all thousands of cars.

claims.claim: The speaker cites Old Dominion Freight Line as an example of an 'invisible moat' built around culture, highlighting its long-term high returns on capital and ability to outperform peers.
claims.quote: And the example I used in that was ODFL, Old Dominion Freight. It's a great company. It's a trucking company. So you would think, you know, there's no way to build a competitive advantage in that business.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Brown and Brown as a company that checks all the boxes from a people standpoint, noting the CEO is third-generation and the CFO is thoughtful.
claims.quote: I mentioned Brown and Brown. I think that's a good example. The CEO is, actually, he's a third generation, which is unusual to have the family's skills go down that far, but he's an excellent CEO.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Copart as a founder-led company where the CEO came up from the business, starting as a teenager and now running the show.
claims.quote: I mentioned Copart. That's another good example because it was a founder-led company. Willis Johnson founded it. Jay Adair is the CEO. And he's another good example because he came up from the business.
